newsitem.title: USA: North Dakota loses ground in fight with Red River.
newsitem.headline: North Dakota loses ground in fight with Red River.

text.p: The Red River rose to the highest levels ever recorded along a 100-mile stretch in North Dakota Thursday, straining dikes to the breaking point and forcing still more residents to flee their homes.

Thousands of weary volunteers, struggling against a flood so big experts said it was a once-in-500-years event, fought to save permanent and temporary levees from south of Fargo upriver to Grand Forks.
Sirens wailed Thursday afternoon in Grand Forks after cracks were found in one clay dike. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers urged residents of a threatened riverside neighbourhood to get out.
The Red rose to 50.37 feet (15.35 metres) at Grand Forks and 39.41 feet (12.01 metres) at Fargo, smashing records set in 1897.
Byron Sieber, a spokesman for the Emergency Operations Centre in Grand Forks, said the dike in question was still holding, although some water was seeping through.
In both Fargo and Grand Rapids sandbagging was continuing around-the-clock. Fargo's streets were crowded with trucks carrying sand, dirt and volunteers.
Deer displaced by the flood invaded one Fargo neighbourhood, foraging for food in garbage cans left uncollected because all garbage workers had been called to flood duty.

Backed-up floodwaters oozed out of manholes on city streets in nearby Moorhead, Minnesota. Officials placed metal plates over the storm sewer covers and parked garbage trucks on top of the plates to keep the water at bay.
At Grand Forks officials earlier had urged a voluntary evacuation of 870 homes and 200 businesses. They said they would need another million sandbags for their battle.

Across the border in Canada preparations were under way to call out military units to deal with the flooding as the northward-flowing Red disgorged a winter's worth of melted snow and ice from the valley.
"No one has ever seen this much water in the Fargo area, ever," said Dennis Walaker, operations manger for Fargo's Public Works Department. "All we can do is react."
Added Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness: "If we're going to go down, we're going to go down fighting." Despite the enormity of the crisis, only 2 percent of the city had actually gone under water, he said.

An urgent call went out Thursday for 1,000 more volunteers in the Fargo area. Fargo police and fire officials went door-to-door through the night in flood-threatened areas advising residents to either evacuate or move possessions to higher elevations.
"Each house is an island out there," Walaker said.
Many of the threatened homes were on Fargo's south side, where some residents chose to stay and ride it out as the Red rose about a quarter inch an hour.
At Grand Forks, 75 miles downstream, Sieber "Everybody is scrambling for moving vans, grain trucks and boxes."
A small boy who was rescued and rescucitated after he apparently fell off the deck of his house into flood waters Wednesday was in fair condition Thursday at a local hospital, Sieber said.

High schools and colleges closed in Grand Forks so students and staff could join residents in sandbagging operations. Joining the effort was the University of North Dakota's national champion men's hockey team and national champion women's basketball team. Personnel from Grand Forks Air Force Base were also put on flood duty.
"We're at 1.5 million (sandbags) this morning and we need another million," Sieber said.

Two of three bridges linking Grand Forks were closed and sandbagging was under way to keep the third open. Grand Forks' United Hospital arranged for an Air Force helicopter to ferry emergency patients in should the third bridge have to be closed, Sieber said.
